newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian artists say forging evidence is kids' stuff.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian artists say forging evidence is kids' stuff.

text.p: "Kompromat:" all purpose Russian word meaning the scandal, the deception, the embarrassing revelations -- and now the exhibition.
A group of Russian artists is trying to show just how dangerously easy modern technology has made the art of forgery.
"Want to ruin your political enemy? Want to boost your newspaper sales? Make your own compromising material!" reads the brochure for the Kompromat exhibition.
"Anyone can forge anything -- the problem is people believe in it," said Marat Gelman, owner of the Moscow gallery where the show is being staged.

Russia has a tradition of rewriting history -- Josef Stalin often doctored photographs to enhance his own image or blot out the memory of murdered rivals. But now computer graphics have put those techniques within the grasp of the man in the street.
Worries about the proliferation of such technology is what prompted the artists to stage the exhibition.

For example, among the displays is a black-and-white photograph of Russia's former public enemy number one, Chechen rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev, chatting casually with ex-Kremlin Security Council secretary, General Alexander Lebed.
Whoops! Lebed was appointed to mediate in Chechnya four months after Dudayev was reported killed in a rocket attack.

The altered image recalls a real-life bid to rewrite history. In January 1995, when Russian troops were storming the Chechen capital Grozny, one newspaper showed a Russian flag flying over Dudayev's presidential palace. Eyewitnesses saw no flag. And Grozny did not fall to the Russians for several weeks.
COMPUTERS MAKE FAKING EASY

"Reality fades and becomes an interpretation of itself," mused Andrei Velikanov, one of the artists running the show. "A schoolboy with a personal computer and a bit of wit can forge any document, even the most sophisticated."

The exhibition includes a range of computer-generated fake documents bearing the seals of all Russia's ministries and other agencies and signed by top officials, including President Boris Yeltsin. There are also forged photos and audio and video tapes.
A credit card issued in the name of the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church, Alexiy II, lies next to lists revealing foreign bank account numbers belonging to leading politicians.

There are also more artistic, bigger items like leather suitcases with luggage labels bearing the names of political leaders. They are packed with compromising material ranging from women's stockings to pornographic photos and even used condoms.
"A scandal takes place and that it is the most important thing," Velikanov said. "They can deny it and check it later, but what people remember is the scandal."

Velikanov shows how Dudayev came back to life on his computer screen. He takes an old photograph of the rebel leader talking to two old men, cuts Lebed's face out of a magazine and pastes it in over one of the men's faces.
"We sharpen the edges and it looks all right," he says.
"But hold on. Lebed is such a tidy, bourgeois general -- he has to have a tie on," he adds. Two minutes later a fancy polka-dot number is hanging from Lebed's collar.
The artists say their message is that people should not be fooled by such tricks, and that the very idea of compromising material, even authentic, is truly dirty.
"If society stops paying attention to it, the phenomenom of kompromat will cease to exist," said Gelman. "They shouldn't take it seriously but treat it with disgust, like mud."

"People sitting in front of their computers should also understand that the stuff they make is dangerous," he added. "Doctors once rejected the idea of changing human DNA on ethical grounds. Maybe it's time to set some ethical limits here."
SCANDAL AS A POLITICAL FACT OF LIFE
"Kompromat" is an important part of Russian political life, buffeting public opinion and leading to scandalous court cases.

Alexander Rutskoi, Yeltsin's former vice-president turned arch-rival during the battle between the Kremlin and parliament in 1993, famously warned he had "11 suitcases of kompromat" against top officials. They never materialised.

Yeltsin's bodyguard, Alexander Korzhakov, was sacked last June and immediately warned he too had files full of "kompromat" against those he believed ousted him, notably new Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

The mud flew again last month when a newspaper published what it said was a transcript of a bugged conversation between Chubais and two other Yeltsin aides, suggesting irregularities in Yeltsin's re-election campaign.
Chubais said the tape was a forgery.

"The tape is on sale here for $500," Gelman said. "Of course, this one is our own forgery. We just put it in a nice box with a good coloured cover to convince people. All this dirt exists because we, people, believe in it."
